nature-econ-719.title: Mixed-strategy equilibria: when randomizing is the answer
nature-econ-719.text: In the game of choosing which side of the road to drive on, there are two obvious equilibria: everyone on the left, or everyone on the right. There is also a third, in which each side is chosen with 50% probability. That is a mixed-strategy Nash equilibrium, one in which at least one player randomizes among strategies with set probabilities. In matching pennies, where one player wins on a match and the other on a mismatch, the only equilibrium is mixed. An equilibrium is strict if every player would lose by switching, and weak if some player is indifferent.

nature-econ-721.title: Nash's theorem: every finite game has an equilibrium
nature-econ-721.text: Nash's theorem guarantees an answer. Every game with finitely many players and finitely many pure strategies has at least one Nash equilibrium, once mixed strategies are allowed. The finiteness matters. When choices are infinite and unbounded, as when two players name numbers and the larger wins, equilibria may fail to exist. Nash's thesis proof used Brouwer's fixed-point theorem; his 1950 paper used the simpler Kakutani fixed-point theorem. Robert Wilson's 1971 oddness theorem adds that almost all finite games have a finite, odd number of Nash equilibria.

nature-econ-720.title: Strong Nash equilibrium: stable against groups
nature-econ-720.text: An ordinary Nash equilibrium only checks whether a single player could gain by switching. That is not convincing enough for cooperative games, where groups can act together. A strong Nash equilibrium is a refinement that is stable against deviations by any coalition of players, not just by individuals. No group can do better by changing course together.

nature-econ-741.title: Axelrod's tournaments: how nice strategies won
nature-econ-741.text: Robert Axelrod organized computer tournaments in which strategies submitted by academics competed in the repeated prisoner's dilemma. Greedy strategies did poorly over the long run, and the simple tit for tat won. Axelrod concluded that successful strategies are nice, retaliating, forgiving and non-envious. He used the results to show how altruism could evolve by natural selection from purely selfish beginnings, reported in his 1984 book The Evolution of Cooperation.

nature-econ-672.title: Four ways to run an auction
nature-econ-672.text: Auctions set prices in a few main ways. In an English auction, bidders openly outbid one another, each bid higher than the last. In a Dutch auction, the auctioneer starts high and lowers the price until someone accepts it or the seller's minimum is reached. In a first-price sealed-bid auction, everyone submits one secret bid at the same time, and the highest bidder pays what they bid. A Vickrey, or second-price sealed-bid, auction works the same way, except that the winner pays the second-highest bid. It is central to auction theory and to online ad bidding.

nature-econ-675.title: Bid rigging: rings that keep prices low
nature-econ-675.text: Bidders who know one another can agree not to compete. In bid rigging, they form a ring whose members avoid bidding against each other, keeping auction prices low. Afterward, ring members may hold their own private auction and split the price difference between the two sales. The practice weakens competition, discourages other bidders and denies the seller the item's true value. Even without an explicit agreement, bidders can in theory coordinate tacitly to keep bids low.

nature-econ-673.title: Reserve prices: the seller's floor
nature-econ-673.text: A reserve price is the minimum a seller sets, below which the auctioned item will not be sold. It protects the seller from a low bid, but it may lower the final price if it dampens interest. The reserve can be announced to bidders or kept secret. In a no-reserve, or absolute, auction the item sells whatever the price, which can draw more bidders hoping for a bargain.

nature-econ-730.title: Crossing out dominated strategies, again and again
nature-econ-730.text: One way to solve a game is to cross out every dominated strategy, then look again. Removing some strategies can make others dominated in the smaller game, so the step repeats until nothing more can go. This iterated elimination relies on rationality being common knowledge: everyone knows that everyone knows, and so on, that all players are rational. With weakly dominated strategies, the result can depend on the order in which they are removed.

nature-econ-681.title: The hawk–dove game: when animals should fight
nature-econ-681.text: Two animals contest a shared resource. Each can fight, playing hawk, or back off, playing dove. This biologists' version of Chicken was first presented, in one form, by John Maynard Smith and George Price in their 1973 paper 'The logic of animal conflict'. Payoffs depend on V, the value of the resource, and C, the cost of an escalated fight, which is almost always assumed larger than V. It is the most commonly used game-theory model of aggression in biology. If one animal can be told apart as territory owner and the other as intruder, role-based pure strategies become evolutionarily stable instead of the mixed one.

nature-econ-683.title: Replicator dynamics: success breeds numbers
nature-econ-683.text: Replicator dynamics is a simple model of how strategies spread in a population, used in evolutionary game theory. A strategy that does better than average grows in frequency, at the expense of those doing worse than average. One version has a single population playing against itself. Another has two populations, each playing only against the other.

nature-econ-686.title: The volunteer's dilemma: someone else should do it
nature-econ-686.text: Each person in a group chooses whether to volunteer. Everyone does best if someone else volunteers, and worst if nobody does. This volunteer's dilemma is one of the many-player games that reduce to Chicken, much as the public goods game reduces to a prisoner's dilemma with two players. Its grim twist concerns numbers: the more players there are, the more likely it is that no one volunteers.

nature-econ-685.title: The war of attrition: who gives up first
nature-econ-685.text: Some contests end not in catastrophe but in exhaustion. In a war of attrition, conflict escalates and outcomes differ only by degree, as each side decides whether the prize is worth the mounting cost of carrying on. That sets it apart from Chicken, where the disastrous outcome differs in kind, such as life against death. In biology it is a very influential model of how contests are settled when physical combat is not possible.

nature-econ-743.title: Non-zero-sum games: when both sides can win
nature-econ-743.text: Two countries swap surplus bananas for surplus apples, and both benefit. That is a non-zero-sum situation: one party's gain need not be another's loss, so the total of gains and losses can be more or less than zero. Positive-sum, or win–win, games are those where the parties' combined gains exceed zero. The prisoner's dilemma is a classic non-zero-sum game. Politics and the economy need not be zero-sum, thanks to cooperation, synergy and economic growth.

nature-econ-744.title: Zero-sum thinking: 'your gain is my loss'
nature-econ-744.text: 'Your gain is my loss' sums up zero-sum thinking, the belief that a situation is zero-sum. Unlike the game-theory concept, it is a psychological construct: a person's subjective reading of a situation. Applying zero-sum logic where it does not fit can breed needless feelings of scarcity and hostility. Economic stagnation can encourage such perceptions, which in turn can raise support for redistribution.

nature-econ-705.title: Anti-coordination games: the cost of following the crowd
nature-econ-705.text: Sometimes doing what others do is the worst choice. In an anti-coordination game, choosing the same action as others creates a cost rather than a benefit, as under negative externalities. Chicken is the best-known two-player example. In a crowding game, each player's payoff falls as more others choose the same strategy, as when extra cars slow a road for everyone. A congestion game is a crowding game in networks. In a discoordination game, one player wants to match and the other to mismatch, so the only equilibrium is mixed; matching pennies is the classic case.

nature-econ-704.title: Coordination failure: settling for the safe option
nature-econ-704.text: Players in a coordination game often end up at a worse equilibrium, because they pick the safer option instead of the one that pays most. Laboratory results suggest this coordination failure is common in stag-hunt and order-statistic games. It is more likely when the risky option's extra reward over the safe one is small. Experience can help. In one weak-link experiment, groups first failed to coordinate, but about 80% coordinated successfully when the game was repeated.

nature-econ-703.title: Focal points: coordinating without talking
nature-econ-703.text: When people must coordinate without talking, they tend to settle on an equilibrium that stands out. That is a focal point. An equilibrium may stand out by paying more, or by being more salient, fairer or safer. These reasons can clash. In the stag hunt, hunting stag together pays more, but hunting hare is safer.

nature-econ-702.title: Voluntary standards: rules people adopt freely
nature-econ-702.text: A voluntary standard is a de facto standard that people adopt freely. It is the typical social-science solution to a coordination problem. Such standards tend to be stable where everyone gains, but only by making mutually consistent choices. A standard enforced by law, called a de jure obligation standard, solves a different problem. That problem is shaped like the prisoner's dilemma.

nature-econ-725.title: Finitely repeated games: how a known end unravels cooperation
nature-econ-725.text: In a finitely repeated game, players repeat a game a fixed, known number of times, and each player's total payoff is the sum over all rounds. A known end is corrosive. If the stage game has a single Nash equilibrium, players play it in every round. Reasoning backward from the last round unravels any cooperation, so cooperation is possible only when the number of rounds is infinite or unknown. The picture changes if the stage game has several equilibria. Then the threat of switching to a worse one later can support cooperation in earlier rounds.

nature-econ-724.title: Trigger strategies: cooperate until crossed
nature-econ-724.text: A trigger strategy cooperates until the other player deviates, then punishes them with play that lowers both players' payoffs. Knowing this, a player expects lower future payoffs if they act selfishly now. An effective trigger makes cooperating worth more than grabbing a gain now and suffering punishment later. The harshest form, grim trigger, punishes forever, and it is used to prove the folk theorem.

nature-econ-688.title: The disagreement point: what happens if talks fail
nature-econ-688.text: Every negotiation has a fallback: the payoffs the parties can expect if talks break down. Game theorists call it the disagreement point. It might be a focal equilibrium both sides expect to play, or zero if no agreement is reached. Because it shapes the final deal, each side gains by raising its own fallback payoff and lowering the other's. That is why it is also called the threat point.

nature-econ-693.title: The egalitarian bargaining solution: equal gains for both
nature-econ-693.text: Ehud Kalai introduced a simple rule for splitting a bargain: give both parties equal gains, by maximizing the smaller of their payoffs. Compared with the Nash bargaining solution, it drops scale invariance, the requirement that changing the units of payoffs leaves the deal unchanged. It keeps independence of irrelevant alternatives and resource monotonicity, the requirement that no one loses when there is more to share. Kalai notes its closeness to the egalitarian ideas of John Rawls.

nature-econ-692.title: The Kalai–Smorodinsky solution: gains in proportion
nature-econ-692.text: The Kalai–Smorodinsky bargaining solution replaces Nash's independence axiom with resource monotonicity. Its rule is proportional: keep the players' gains in the same ratio as their maximum possible gains. With the disagreement point at zero, it picks the efficient point whose payoffs stand in the ratio of each player's best achievable gain. A player who could hope for more therefore receives more.

nature-econ-690.title: The Nash demand game: ask too much and lose everything
nature-econ-690.text: Two players each demand a share of a good. Both get their demands only if the total does not exceed what is available. This Nash demand game has many Nash equilibria: any pair of demands that adds up exactly to the whole is one. Both players demanding everything is also an equilibrium, though both then get nothing. When uncertainty about feasible payoffs vanishes, its equilibrium payoffs converge to the Nash bargaining solution.

nature-econ-691.title: The Rubinstein model: bargaining over a shrinking pie
nature-econ-691.text: In the Rubinstein bargaining model, players take turns proposing how to split a surplus, and the surplus shrinks with every round of delay. The model has a single subgame perfect equilibrium, and its division depends on how strongly players prefer payoffs now over later. That preference is captured by a discount factor d, the value today of a payoff one round away. With the surplus set to 1, player 1 gets 1/(1+d) and player 2 gets d/(1+d). As players become perfectly patient, the split converges to the Nash bargaining solution.
